title: The happy sleeper
hookLine: Hatthaka asks the Buddha if he slept well on the frozen ground; yes, better than anyone (AN 3.34)

cards: Frost on the ground. Leaves sparse on the trees. A cold wind blowing.
That's the winter night the Anguttara describes, near the town of Alavi. In the morning a man named Hatthaka, out walking, finds the Buddha beside a cattle track, sitting on a thin spread of leaves.
So Hatthaka asks what anyone asks a guest in the morning: did you sleep well? Yes, the Buddha says. I'm one of those in the world who sleep well.

teach.b: First, the doubt. Hatthaka lists it all back: cold winter nights, ground trampled hard by cattle hooves, a thin spread of leaves, thin robes, a cold wind. How could anyone sleep well out here?
Second, the counter-question. Let me ask you something, the Buddha says, and answer as you like.
Take a householder with a fine house, plastered inside and out, closed against the wind, its door bolted and its windows shut. A couch spread with long-fleeced woolen covers. A lamp burning.
People attending him. Would he sleep well? Yes, says Hatthaka.
Third, the turn. And if a fever of lust arose in him, or hatred, or delusion, burning in body and mind, would he sleep badly? Yes, he would.
Fourth, the end of the fever.

teach.h: THE FEVER THAT KEEPS HIM UP.
teach.b: Those burnings, the very things that keep the comfortable man awake, the Buddha says, have been abandoned in him, cut off at the root like a palm stump that can't grow again.

teach.h: CUT OFF LIKE A PALM STUMP.
teach.b: So he sleeps well, even on frozen leaves. The discourse ends in a verse: the one who is fully at peace sleeps at ease, cooled, with nothing left to burn. It isn't a teaching against beds, or houses, or blankets.
It's a question about what actually keeps a person awake.

how: Monks and nuns in the forest traditions sometimes sleep simply, on a mat or the ground, and some Buddhists recall the Buddha's posture of lying on the right side, mindful, as they go to sleep.

o: cold, the chill of a winter night
sleep, the rest that comes at night

games.q: a cold night: tap the pairs.
p: a thin spread of leaves by a cattle track
a fever of lust, hatred or delusion

s: the Buddha admitted it had been a hard night
he said he was one of those in the world who sleep well.
in the story, the rich man sleeps badly when a fever of hatred arises
a warm house can't cool that fever.
the teaching says comfortable beds are wrong
it asks what really keeps a person awake.

games.q: you're Hatthaka. you've just told the Buddha nobody could sleep well on frozen ground in this wind. how does he answer?
o: he asks you about a rich man in a warm house.
he tells you to try it yourself.
games.why: he asks about a householder in a fine, closed house: would he sleep badly if a fever of lust, hatred or delusion burned in him? yes. those fevers are gone in the Buddha, so he sleeps well.

practice: Ask Hatthaka's question of your own nights: what actually keeps me up? Maybe not the mattress; maybe a worry, a grudge, the pull of one more scroll, and if something comes, name it gently, without trying to fix it.
Then let a few slow breaths go out, the way they might once your head is on the pillow.

wordCard.voice: Sukha, ease. What the Buddha says he sleeps in, even on frozen ground, because nothing in him is left burning. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sukha: ease, happiness; the Buddha says he sleeps at ease, sukham.

carryVoice: Your line: I sleep well. Ease, here, has more to do with the mind than the bed. Rest well.
